extracted.intended_audience: filmmakers, parents, distributors, journalists, and researchers interested in the U.S. Motion Picture Association (MPA) film rating system
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards used by the Motion Picture Association (MPA) / Classification & Ratings Administration (CARA) to classify motion pictures and related promotional materials in the United States, including rating definitions, content components, trailer/ad guidelines, and procedural/impact considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: G – General Audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: All ages admitted. Nothing that would offend parents for viewing by children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: G-rated films do not receive content descriptors (content is considered suitable for all audiences even if it contains mildly-objectionable content).

rubrics_metrics.name: PG – Parental Guidance Suggested
rubrics_metrics.description: Some material may not be suitable for children. Parents urged to give "parental guidance". May contain some material parents might not like for their young children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content descriptors (brief descriptions of specifics behind the film's content and why it received a certain rating) may be used for PG-rated films.

rubrics_metrics.name: PG-13 – Parents Strongly Cautioned
rubrics_metrics.description: Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13. Parents are urged to be cautious. Some material may be inappropriate for pre-teenagers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduced to cover films that are not suitable for all children but not adult/restricted; content descriptors apply; certain uses of language, nudity, or violence may trigger PG-13 rather than PG.

rubrics_metrics.name: R – Restricted
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian. Contains some adult material. Parents are urged to learn more about the film before taking their young children with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R indicates adult material that may include stronger language, sex, nudity, drug use, or intense violence; enforcement practices (e.g., theater policies, R-cards) and appeals/edits can affect distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: NC-17 – Adults Only
rubrics_metrics.description: No one 17 and under admitted. Clearly adult. Children are not admitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NC-17 replaced the non-trademarked X rating; carries substantial commercial stigma (limits advertising, theatrical bookings, and retail stocking), leading many filmmakers/studios to recut films to achieve an R rating. In practice the label has significant market consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content descriptors (rating explanations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brief descriptions of the specifics behind the film's content and why it received a certain rating; displayed in trailers, posters, and on home-video packaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptors are used for films rated from PG to NC-17 (not for G). They provide parents with specifics (e.g., "some sexual content", "strong language", "graphic violence"). The MPA began including explanations for PG, PG-13, and NC-17-rated films in the early 2000s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not Rated / Unrated / "This Film Is Not Yet Rated" labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Labels used when a film has not been submitted for a rating or is an uncut version of a submitted film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unrated/Uncut versions often carry warnings that content differs from the theatrical release and may not be suitable for minors. Trailers or ads may use "This Film Is Not Yet Rated" prior to final assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of promotional materials – Green band (trailers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Green band cards indicate trailers approved to accompany a feature or approved for appropriate audiences online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Green band wording varies: when trailer accompanies another rated feature the band says it is "approved to accompany this feature"; for internet trailers wording is tweaked to "approved for appropriate audiences." Historically signified adherence to MPAA advertising standards (limits on foul language, violent/sexual imagery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of promotional materials – Yellow band (trailers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Yellow band was introduced for internet-hosted trailers with restricted content, carrying the message "The following preview has been approved only for age-appropriate Internet users."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPAA stipulated yellow-band online trailers should be available between 9:00 p.m. and 4:00 a.m. or hosted on sites whose typical user base is at least 80% adults. Reserved for trailers previewing PG-13 or stronger. Yellow bands were not widely adopted and were largely abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulation of promotional materials – Red band (trailers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Red title card is issued to trailers which do not adhere to MPA/CARA guidelines and signals approval for restricted or mature audiences only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserved for trailers previewing R and NC-17 rated films (may include nudity, profanity, or other material deemed inappropriate for children). Red-band trailers are meant to be age-gated on the internet and may be shown theatrically only before R, NC-17, or unrated movies; however, age-verification is often ineffective in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blue feature tags (theatrical & home media releases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blue feature tags contain the rating block and any content descriptors, the MPA logo, and links; theatrical releases show the blue tag after the film, home media releases show it before the film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to display the official rating and descriptors on the feature itself as assigned by CARA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violence guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: Depictions of violence are permitted under all ratings but must be moderated for the lower ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violence must be kept to a minimum in G-rated films and must not be intense in PG-rated films. Depictions of intense violence are permitted under PG-13, but violence that is both realistic and extreme or persistent will generally require at least an R rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language guideline (including the 'automatic language rule')
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for profanity and expletives across ratings; 'automatic language rule' references how certain words affect ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: G: no stronger words present. PG: mild profanity may be present. Use of the word "fuck" will initially incur at least a PG-13 rating; more than one occurrence will usually incur an R rating and sexual-context uses are treated more harshly. Exceptions to the automatic language rule can be made if two-thirds of board members agree context justifies a PG-13. The rule is a common ground for appeals and edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substances (drug use & tobacco) guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: Depictions of drug use and tobacco are considered when assigning ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drug use content is restricted to PG-13 and above. Since May 2007, depictions of cigarette smoking are considered as a factor in a film's rating; anti-smoking advocates have argued smoking depiction should affect child-appropriate ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nudity guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: Nudity is restricted to PG and above; sexually-oriented nudity typically requires an R rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anything that constitutes more than brief nudity will require at least a PG-13 rating. Since 2006 films have been flagged for carrying nudity (including specifying male nudity or partial nudity where relevant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex content guideline
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no explicit, detailed MPAA criteria for sexual content beyond excluding sex scenes from G-rated films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sex scenes are permitted at PG and above, but sexual content intensity and context influence whether a film is rated PG-13, R, or NC-17; historically sex has often led to stricter ratings than comparable violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary nature of the rating system and exhibition practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The MPA rating system is a voluntary scheme not enforced by law; films can be exhibited without a rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most theaters refuse to exhibit non-rated or NC-17 films, so commercial practice effectively enforces ratings. Non-members of the MPA may also submit films for rating. Local or state laws (and theater policies) can create variations in enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age thresholds & jurisdictional variances
rubrics_metrics.description: Age cutoffs associated with ratings (e.g., R under-17 accompaniment requirement; NC-17 disallows 17 and under).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R: under 17 requires accompanying parent/guardian (historically ages changed over time). NC-17: no one 17 and under admitted (1996 wording clarified). Jurisdictions have sometimes enacted differing rules (e.g., Tennessee at one point set R minimum age to 18) but laws can be subject to constitutional challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edits and appeals process to change ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Studios and filmmakers may edit films or appeal CARA decisions to obtain a different rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many films have been re-cut to obtain a milder rating (e.g., edits to avoid NC-17). Appeals can succeed (examples: Bully, Philomena, Blue Valentine on appeal), while some filmmakers choose to release unrated rather than accept certain ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: R-card and exhibition exceptions (theater-issued cards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theater initiatives (e.g., R Cards) allowing minors to see R-rated films without adult accompaniment have been attempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R Cards (introduced by GKC Theatres in 2004) were controversial; MPA and theater organizations argued they distort the intent of the ratings and that R covers a broad range of films, so such cards may be harmful or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and publicizing standards (critic demand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics and filmmakers have argued the MPA should reveal rating standards and specific reasons for decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for publicizing standards stem from perceived opacity (MPA does not reveal how/why decisions are made or which specific scenes need cuts), which critics say undermines trust and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency across studios and independent films (bias concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that major studio releases may receive more lenient treatment than independent films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited where independents received harsher ratings for similar content; concerns include perceived industry influence because studios fund the MPAA and may have leverage. This is a criterion critics use when evaluating fairness of the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratings creep (temporal consistency of categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: The concern that the amount of sex, violence, and profanity tolerated in each rating category has increased over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies (e.g., Harvard School of Public Health) have found increases in profanity, sex, and violence across years within the same rating categories; critics cite this as erosion of category meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial consequences and marketability of ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: How a rating affects a film's ability to be advertised, booked in theaters, and sold in retail/outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NC-17 in particular is described as a 'kiss of death' because many theaters, media outlets, and retailers refuse to carry or advertise such films; this economic impact influences producers' decisions to edit for lower ratings or avoid theatrical releases.
